18 June, evening, Bucharest. The club has gathered at Ana’s. In the morning Marta called Ecaterina: Andrés died peacefully in his sleep. Ana, Andrei and Mihai want to write to Marta and Pilar.
We have to write to Marta and Pilar. But I don’t even know how to start. “Hi, I’m sorry” sounds awful.
For Pilar, who hardly knows us, something formal is better: “Dear Pilar, we wish to express our deepest condolences.”
And for Marta, something warmer. She’s almost family by now.
Yes, and then something personal. A concrete memory. The worst thing about condolence letters is that they all sound the same.
I remember the day of the fair, when he greeted the audience as if he were a minister.
And the bit about the lorry driver who cried in Hungary. Costel says it’s the nicest thing anyone has ever said to him.
Then we’ll put that: “We will never forget the day when…”. And at the end: “We’re here for anything you need.”
And Ecaterina? Do we write to her too?
You don’t write Ecaterina a letter. You take Ecaterina soup. Costel has already called Mrs Florica.

Ecaterina had her cataract operation on 10 June, at eight in the morning, in a Bucharest hospital. The operation took twenty minutes. Ana waited for her in the corridor with a flask of coffee and a book she couldn’t manage to read. The next day, when they took off the bandage, the first thing Ecaterina saw was the book she had left on the bedside table: “Librăria de pe strada Huertas”. The cover was dark blue. Not grey, as she had seen it for months, but blue. Ecaterina burst into tears, and the doctor, worried, asked whether it hurt. She told him no, she was crying because blue was blue.

She walked home, although Ana wanted to call a taxi. She looked at everything as if she had just arrived in the city: the leaves of the lime trees on the boulevard, the cracks in the buildings, the colours of the trams, people’s faces. At home she looked at herself in the mirror for a long time. Then she told Ana that the doctor had promised she would see better, but nobody had warned her she would also see herself. Ana laughed. So did Ecaterina.

In the afternoon Rosa Elena came. She climbed onto the sofa, held Ecaterina’s face in both hands and examined her eyes very closely, with the seriousness of an eye doctor. Then she asked whether she could now see the little letters in storybooks. Ecaterina took a book from the shelf and read her a whole story without glasses, for the first time in two years. When she had finished, Rosa Elena declared that the operation had been a success and that the doctor deserved a drawing.

On 12 June they made a video call to Madrid. Andrés was in bed, very thin, and Marta was holding the tablet. Speaking was hard for him, but when he saw Ecaterina his eyes opened wide and he asked whether she could see well. She told him she could see him perfectly and that he looked older. He replied that she, on the other hand, looked prettier, and that it must be the operation. They talked for only five minutes, because he tired quickly. Before hanging up, Andrés said a single word: “Write.”

And Ecaterina wrote. It was the first real letter she had written to him in forty years: by hand, with a fountain pen, on writing paper she had to buy at a stationer’s in the centre because she had none left at home. It took her three days to finish it. She wrote about the blue of the cover, about the leaves of the lime trees, about Rosa Elena, who could already write her name in Spanish. She didn’t write about the past. On 14 June she took it to the post office and sent it express.

The letter reached the calle del Prado on the morning of 17 June. Marta read it to her grandfather in the afternoon, slowly, sitting by the bed. Andrés listened with his eyes closed. When Marta finished, he smiled and said: “At last it has arrived.” Marta didn’t know whether he was talking about that letter or another, one that had taken forty years to arrive. That night Andrés fell asleep with Rosa Elena’s drawing on the bedside table, the one of the book lorry.

On 18 June, at seven in the morning, the phone rang at Ecaterina’s. She knew what it was before she answered. Marta told her, her voice breaking, that Andrés had died at dawn, in his sleep, without pain, in peace. Ecaterina only said: “Thank you for telling me yourself.” Then she hung up and sat by the window for an hour, without crying. Afterwards she went to the kitchen and made coffee for two, out of a habit from another century. When she realised, she stood looking at the two cups and then, yes, she cried.

The news spread at once. Ana arrived first, holding Rosa Elena’s hand. Then Andrei came. At midday the doorbell rang: it was Mrs Florica, Costel’s neighbour, with a pot of soup still hot. Costel had called her at eight from a car park in Poland. He hadn’t managed to say anything; he just cried. Mrs Florica had taken the phone from her own husband, understood what was happening and started cooking without asking any more questions.

Ecaterina decided to go to the funeral. The doctor allowed it on three conditions: sunglasses, drops every four hours and no carrying suitcases. Ana offered to go with her and carry the suitcases for both of them. Mihai stayed in Bucharest with Rosa Elena, who that afternoon made another drawing: the book lorry climbing up to heaven, loaded to the top. When they asked her why it was so full, she explained it was so that Señor Andrés would have something to read.

On the plane, Ecaterina didn’t read. She looked at the clouds the whole flight, with her new eyes, as if she wanted to learn their shapes. At one point she told Ana that for forty years she had imagined her return to Madrid many times, in a thousand different ways, but never like this: with sunglasses, a bottle of drops in her handbag and a black dress Mrs Florica had lent her, because her own had become too big. Ana squeezed her hand and said nothing, because there was nothing to say.

They arrived in Madrid on 19 June. It was hot, but Ecaterina insisted on walking from the metro to the calle del Prado. With her new eyes, the city looked different: the ochre of the façades, the red of the geraniums on the balconies, the almost white blue of the sky. When Pilar opened the door of the flat, the two women hugged without hesitating this time. Behind Pilar, in the hallway, the green sign shone with an intensity Ecaterina didn’t remember.

The funeral took place on 20 June at the Almudena cemetery. The family expected about twenty people. More than a hundred and fifty came. Carmen and Juan were there, the director of the fair, several retired booksellers and dozens of readers who had seen the news in the paper. Lola had closed the café and hung a sign on the door: “Closed for mourning. Back tomorrow, with more books.”

Many of those who came brought a book bought at La Lámpara, with the bookshop’s stamp on the first page. A very old gentleman showed a book of poems from 1975, still wrapped in the bookshop’s brown paper, because he had never dared to open it. A woman said she had met her husband in the poetry section, and that Andrés had given them the book they both wanted to buy at the same time. The books piled up on a table, beside the flowers, until they formed a small bookshop.

Marta said little. She said her novel wasn’t hers but her grandfather’s; she had only put in the commas. Pilar said her father sold books but, above all, gave them away. Then someone asked Ecaterina to say a few words. She shook her head. But she came forward, took off her sunglasses and recited the Machado poem, the one by the lake in the Retiro, slowly, looking at the flowers. This time she didn’t skip a single line.

At that same hour, in a car park near Poznań, Costel got down from his lorry with the old road atlas in his hand and stood in silence for a minute. Two other lorry drivers who were having coffee came over to ask if something was wrong. When Costel explained, in a mixture of Polish, English and gestures, they both took off their caps and stayed with him. Zoltán did the same at a petrol station near Budapest. Both of them sent Marta a photo.

At the end of the ceremony, nobody knew what to do with the books. Nobody wanted to take them home again, but nobody wanted to leave them there either. It was Marta who decided: she gave them to Lola, for the café’s shelves. She said that way the bookshop would stay open, even if only in a corner and even if the books were now lent instead of sold. Lola, who had held back her tears all morning, burst out crying then, hugging a box full of books wrapped in brown paper.

In the afternoon, back at the flat, Marta gave Ecaterina a parcel wrapped in brown paper, like the bookshop’s. On the paper, in shaky handwriting, it said: “For E., when I am gone.” Marta explained that her grandfather had prepared it on 3 June, the good morning, after Ecaterina had read to him. He had asked Marta for the paper, the string and a pen, and had taken over an hour to make the parcel, because he wanted it to look the way it used to.

Inside was Rayuela. Andrés’s copy, with his underlinings from 1979. Between the pages was still Ecaterina’s 1987 letter, the one she had read him in December. But there was something else: a second envelope, yellowed, sealed, with two handwritten words: “To E.”. It had no address. Marta told her that envelope had always been in the drawer of her grandfather’s bedside table, and that on the afternoon of 3 June he had asked her to put it in the book. She had never opened it.

Ecaterina didn’t open it there. She asked Ana to go with her to calle de las Huertas. Lola, who had just come back from the cemetery, opened up the closed café for them and gave them the table at the back, by the window, without asking questions. Ecaterina sat exactly where the counter used to be. She knew, without anyone telling her, that Andrés had written that letter there, standing, leaning on the dark wood, one autumn night in 1987.

The letter was short. It said: “E.: I don’t know where to send this letter, so I will keep it. If you ever come back, you will find it. I’m not asking for explanations. I only want you to know that I’m not angry, and that the lamp stays lit. Every night. Until you come back or until I go, whichever happens first. A.” The date was 2 November 1987. Ecaterina read it once in silence and again aloud, for Ana. Her voice didn’t shake.

Then she sat looking at the two envelopes, side by side, on the table. Hers had waited almost forty years in a drawer in Bucharest; his, forty in a drawer in Madrid. Two letters written the same autumn, in two cities, never sent because neither of them had dared. Now they were together, inside the same book. Ecaterina said to Ana: “It took them forty years to find each other. Like us.”

That night, Ecaterina slept in the flat on the calle del Prado, in the room off the hallway. She woke at three in the morning and couldn’t get back to sleep. She got up without a sound and stood for a while in the hallway, in front of the green sign, lit only by the streetlight. She touched it with her fingertips, the way you touch the face of someone sleeping. Then she went back to bed, with the two envelopes under her pillow, and slept until ten.

On 21 June, the day she flew back to Bucharest, Marta received an email from the city council: it had been decided to authorise the installation of the commemorative plaque. Marta forwarded it to Ecaterina with a single comment: “In the end it came too late. He said the council would have to wait, but he was the one who couldn’t wait.” Ecaterina laughed for the first time in three days. Then she slowly typed on her phone the text she was proposing for the plaque.

It was just two sentences: “Here stood the La Lámpara bookshop. Its bookseller, Andrés Gil, left the light on.” Marta replied a minute later with a single word: “Perfect.” Lola, whom Marta showed it to that same afternoon, said there was no need to wait for the plaque: that night, when she closed the café, she left the lamp at the back on, the one where the counter used to be. And she promised to leave it on every night.

In Bucharest, Ecaterina put Rayuela on her desk, next to the blue book, with the two letters inside. Rosa Elena gave her the drawing of the lorry climbing to heaven, and she hung it above the desk. That night, for the first time in months, she switched on the computer, opened a blank document and sat looking at it for a long time. She didn’t yet know what she was going to write. But she knew she would write it with her new eyes, and that somewhere in Madrid a lamp was still lit.
